## Hypergraph Introduction and History

Hypergraphs were introduced in 1973 by Berge. More specifically, Berge introduces hypergraphs in works from 1967 and 1973 as a means to generalize the graph approach.

The foundational work was published as a book: The original edition was published in 1970 with the title "Graphes et hypergraphes", and a revised edition was published in English in 1973 by North-Holland Pub. Co.

## Purpose and Significance

Graphs only support pairwise relationships, while hypergraphs preserve the multi-adic relationships and become a natural modeling of collaboration networks and various other situations.

## References on Hypergraph Theory

Further details on hypergraphs can be found in Berge [1967, 1973], in Voloshin [2009] or in Bretto [2013]. result: {"query":"tungara frog Ryan Rand female choice call complexity rival male chuck Physalaemus pustulosus","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_01EwP4bLhdo55DgRVq46ie1L","content":[{"title":"sciencedaily.com","url":"https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2006/05/060504065752.htm"},{"title":"Frogs: Female choice for complex calls led to evolution of unusual male vocal cord","url":"https://phys.org/news/2006-05-frogs-female-choice-complex-evolution.html"},{"title":"In túngara frogs, female choice for complex calls led to evolution of unusual male vocal cord","url":"https://news.mongabay.com/2006/05/in-tungara-frogs-female-choice-for-complex-calls-led-to-evolution-of-unusual-male-vocal-cord/"},{"title":"Even humans love a good mating call","url":"https://www.popsci.com/environment/mating-call-humans-animals/"},{"title":"Volume 121, Issue 8 pp. 749-759","url":"https://onlinelibrary-wiley-com-443.webvpn.zafu.edu.cn/doi/abs/10.1111/eth.12387"},{"title":"par.nsf.gov","url":"https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10554926"},{"title":"Mate choice in response to dynamic presentation of male advertisement signals in Tungara frogs","url":"https://repository.si.edu/items/b9d29b51-0141-48f3-aa78-e7f52cc09620"},{"title":"courses.washington.edu","url":"https://courses.washington.edu/ccab/Ron08TungaraFrogs.pdf"},{"title":"Modeling sexual selection in Túngara frog and rationality of mate choice","url":"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1610.03930"}]},"Based on the search results, here's what I found about túngara frogs, female choice, call complexity, and the researchers involved:

## Key Research Findings

Dr. Mike Ryan of The University of Texas at Austin, Dr. Marcos Gridi-Papp, and the late Dr. Stan Rand published findings in Nature about how female túngara frogs choose mates based on call complexity.

Males of the túngara frog, Physalaemus pustulosus, attract females by singing "whine chuck chuck" calls, and females are more attracted to males that also produce chucks.

## The Evolution Connection

Male túngara frogs have evolved masses on their vocal cords that help them produce complex calls, which scientists discovered by surgically removing the fibrous masses and finding they could no longer produce the "chuck".

The fibrous masses on male vocal cords evolved in response to female preference, with female preferences indirectly shaping the anatomy of the male calling apparatus.

## Effects of Rival Males

Decision making during mate choice is sensitive to interruption from competing signallers, and females actively compare multiple signallers simultaneously, with commitment to an initial mate approach depending on whether there is a state change in signal complexity."],"durationSeconds":6.13535233299993,"searchCount":1}

result: {"query":"tala Indian music rhythmic cycle definition Natyashastra tala meaning clap cycle avartana scholarship","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_01JzpTPNs3AfnTRZbCCNJA2A","content":[{"title":"Tala (music)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tala_(music)"},{"title":"Atatala, Ata-tala: 2 definitions","url":"https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/atatala"},{"title":"chromatone.center","url":"https://chromatone.center/theory/rhythm/system/tala/"},{"title":"Tala (music)","url":"https://wikipedia.com/wiki/Thalam"},{"title":"Introduction Tala","url":"https://www.tosslevy.nl/tabla/talas/"},{"title":"Tāla: Features of Rhythm System in Indian Classical Music","url":"https://www.zurnalai.vu.lt/acta-orientalia-vilnensia/article/view/18351"},{"title":"top of page","url":"https://www.agnirva.com/learn/what-is-a-tala-(rhythmic-pattern)%3F"},{"title":"narthaki.com","url":"https://narthaki.com/info/snippets/snpaug12.html"},{"title":"Sayak Mitra","url":"https://naadnartan.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Sayak-Mitra.pdf"}]},"Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about tala in Indian music:

## Definition and Etymology

Tala literally means a "clap, tapping one's hand on one's arm, a musical measure", and in Sanskrit, tala means the palm of the hand, clapping of hands, rhythm. It is the term used in Indian classical music to refer to musical meter, that is any rhythmic beat or strike that measures musical time.

## Rhythmic Cycle Structure

A tala is a rhythmic structure of a number of measures that forms a rhythmic cycle, a rhythmic phrase that is repeated over and over. A metric cycle of a tala contains a specific number of beats, which can be as short as 3 beats or as long as 128 beats. The length of a cycle of a tala is called avarta.

## Foundational Role in Indian Music

The tala as the time cycle, and the raga as the melodic framework, are the two foundational elements of classical Indian music.

## Natyashastra Connection

The oldest books on Indian music like Bharata's "Natyasastra" and Dattila's "Dattilam" from around 2000 years ago both considered tala as an indispensable principled element in Indian music. According to the Natyashastra tradition, talas had three basic time units Laghu, Guru and Pluta, with Laghu being one Matra, Guru being two Matras and Pluta being three Matras.

## Elements of Tala

The beats within each rhythmic cycle are called matras, and the first beat of any rhythmic cycle is called the sam. An empty beat is called khali."],"durationSeconds":7.700108083998784,"searchCount":1}

## Liu Hui's Circle Area Proof

Liu Hui rigorously proved algorithms for determining the area of circles and the volume of pyramids by dissecting the regions into infinitely many pieces. In his commentary to The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, Liu Hui remarked that the ratio of the circumference of an inscribed hexagon to the diameter of the circle was three, hence π must be greater than three, and he provided a detailed step-by-step description of an iterative algorithm to calculate π to any required accuracy based on bisecting polygons.

Liu Hui, in his commentary, discusses a "method of exhaustion" he has invented to find the correct formula for the volume of a pyramid. This method of exhaustion, which involved dividing shapes into infinitely many pieces and using a limiting process, was a precursor to calculus concepts.

## Context

Liu Hui completed his commentary in 263 on The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, and his commentary proved the correctness of its algorithms—these proofs are the earliest-known Chinese proofs in the contemporary sense.

## Overview

The origins of anekāntavāda can be traced back to the teachings of Mahāvīra (599–527 BCE), the 24th Jain Tīrthankara.

## The Three Key Concepts

**Anekantavada:** The doctrine of anekāntavāda holds that truth and reality are complex and always have multiple aspects. The word anekantavada was coined by Acharya Siddhasen Divakar to denote the teachings of Mahavira that state truth can be expressed in infinite ways.

**Syadvada and Nayavada:** The dialectical concepts of syādvāda "conditioned viewpoints" and nayavāda "partial viewpoints" arose from anekāntavāda in the medieval era, providing Jainism with more detailed logical structure and expression.

## Historical Development

The details of the doctrine emerged in Jainism in the 1st millennium CE, from debates between scholars of Jain, Buddhist and Vedic schools of philosophies. ## Overview of Karaka Theory

The Kāraka in Sanskrit grammar traces the relation between a noun and a verb in a sentence structure. Pāṇini neologized the term Kāraka in the sūtra Kārake (1.4.23, Astadhyayi).

The word Kāraka refers to 'that which brings about' or 'doer'. Pāṇini has used the term Kāraka for a syntactico-semantic relation, used as an intermediary step to express the semantic relations through the usage of vibhaktis (case markers).

## Function in Grammar

As per the doctrine of Pāṇini, the rules pertaining to Kāraka explain a situation in terms of action (kriyā) and factors (kārakas), both of which play an important function to denote the accomplishment of the action.

Pāṇini's grammar Aṣtādhyāyī ('Eight Chapters') is crucially based on the notion of 'kāraka', generally translated as 'semantic role'.

## Historical Significance

Since ancient times Kāraka theory has been used to analyze the Sanskrit language, and due to its efficiency and flexibility the Pāṇinian grammatical model was adopted for formal representation in other Indian languages as well.

## The Coining of "Synapse" (1897)

Sherrington introduced the term synapse in 1897 when Michael Foster invited him to revise the chapters on the nervous system for the seventh edition of his Textbook of Physiology.

## The Role of Verrall

The surname in your query—Verrall—refers to Arthur Woolgar Verrall, a Euripidean scholar and professor of English at Trinity College, who suggested 'synapse' (from συναπτω) after Sherrington wrote Foster of his difficulty and desire to introduce a specific name, initially suggesting syndesm, but Foster consulted Verrall who suggested 'synapse' and as that yields a better adjectival form, it was adopted for the book.

## Foster and Integration

Charles Sherrington, Foster's former pupil, deserves much credit for not only creating the word itself but also for advocating the concept of a synapse, most notably from his work on physiological reflexes. The Silliman Lectures introduced the term integration into scientific neurology, and Sherrington's masterpiece, The integrative action of the nervous system (1906), established neuron theory and introduced the concept of proprioception."],"durationSeconds":6.30093083300069,"searchCount":1}

## Key Points from the Search Results:

**The Famous Sentence and Autonomy of Syntax:**

Chomsky offered "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" as an example of a grammatically correct sentence that has no discernible meaning, thus arguing for the independence of syntax from semantics. This sentence demonstrates that, in order for a sentence to be syntactically correct, it does not need to be coherent or meaningful in any way.

**The Argument Against Statistical Models:**

An important clarification: Chomsky was arguing that "the notion of [the probability of a sentence] is an entirely useless one" and devised a sentence which certainly was not part of any corpus, arguing that this was supposed to prove that statistical models of language (i.e., Markov models) were hopelessly inept at explaining language.

**Syntactic Structures:**

Chomsky's 1957 Syntactic Structures is an argument for the existence of syntax as both necessary for a full account of language, and as independent of other aspects of language, with arguments that grammaticality cannot be explained by appeal to either probabilistic or semantic factors.

**The Principle of Autonomy:**

The autonomy of syntax does not entail that grammaticality is cut off from either probability or meaning, but rather says that syntax cannot be reduced to either of these.

result: {"query":"Anne Sullivan Helen Keller well-house April 5 1887 water scholarship Keller's earlier language, Story of My Life Sullivan letters","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_018tt8ie944mWiMxX6yAxp6w","content":[{"title":"A Little Happier: Teacher Anne Sullivan Writes About Hellen Keller’s Moment of Profound Realization","url":"https://gretchenrubin.com/podcast-episode/little-happier-teacher-anne-sullivan/"},{"title":"embarking on an educational journey how anne sullivan taught helen keller","url":"https://aph.org/blog/embarking-on-an-educational-journey-how-anne-sullivan-taught-helen-keller"},{"title":"bio001200301 01 0003","url":"https://dbnl.org/tekst/_bio001200301_01/_bio001200301_01_0003.php"},{"title":"Your 1 Good Thing","url":"https://y1gt.alitu.com/episode/af9925f3-06e3-4842-a2a7-38ca1024ac71"},{"title":"www.afb.org","url":"https://www.afb.org/node/13808"},{"title":"teaching helen","url":"https://afb.org/about-afb/history/online-museums/anne-sullivan-miracle-worker/anne-teacher/teaching-helen"},{"title":"on this day helen keller comprehends the word water","url":"https://findingdulcinea.com/on-this-day-helen-keller-comprehends-the-word-water/"},{"title":"karsh.org","url":"https://karsh.org/?p=20908"},{"title":"Helen Keller: A Champion of Education and Advocacy","url":"https://skillnation.in/posts/helen-keller-education-background/"}]},"Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about Anne Sullivan, Helen Keller, and the historic water pump moment:

## The Historic Breakthrough

On April 5, 1887, at a water pump outside the Keller home in Tuscumbia, Alabama, Helen made her famous breakthrough — connecting the word "water" spelled into her hand with the substance flowing over her skin.

## Anne Sullivan's Account

Anne Sullivan wrote to Sophia Hopkins on April 5, 1887, about the same incident, providing a detailed first-hand account. Helen had taken the second great step in her education: she had learned that everything has a name, and that the manual alphabet is the key to everything she wants to know.

Sullivan described the moment vividly: They went out to the pump-house, and Anne made Helen hold her mug under the spout while she pumped. As the cold water gushed forth, filling the mug, she spelled "w-a-t-e-r" in Helen's free hand. The word coming so close upon the sensation of cold water rushing over her hand seemed to startle her. She dropped the mug and stood as one transfixed. A new light came into her face.

## Helen Keller's Earlier Language Struggles

Before this breakthrough, Anne had written that "mug" and "milk" had given Helen more trouble than all the rest. She confused the nouns with the verb "drink." She didn't know the word for "drink," but went through the pantomime of drinking whenever she spelled "mug" or "milk."

## Impact

From that moment, Helen demanded to learn everything. Within months, she knew hundreds of words and could form simple sentences."],"durationSeconds":7.983180750001222,"searchCount":1}

The Wikipedia article provides minimal detail on *sāmānya*, describing it only as "the classicism of the substances i.e. *papa*, *apara,* *parapara*." The article does not explain how cognition of generality arises.

## Kāṇāda's Original Padārthas

The article indicates that **abhāva (non-existence) was a later addition**. It states: "The *bhāva padārthas* are of six types, while abhāva was added later" and notes that abhāva was "added by later Vaiśeṣika scholars such as Śrīdhara, Udayana and Śivāditya."

This suggests Kāṇāda's original system contained six categories (substance, quality, activity, generality, particularity, and inherence), with non-existence appended subsequently.

## Scholarly Citations

The article cites Umesh Mishra's *Conception of Matter according to Nyayavaisesika* (1987) and references from Wisdom Library regarding these categorizations, though it lacks detailed philosophical analysis of how each category functions or how their cognition develops.","durationMs":4439,"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padārtha"}

result: {"bytes":304706,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Ganges River Dolphin Echolocation and Vision

**Vision:**
The dolphin has severely limited eyesight. "Their eyes are usually small due to the cloudy water," and it is described as effectively blind in its murky river habitat.

**Echolocation Use:**
The dolphin relies heavily on echolocation to navigate and find food. It "produces an ultrasonic sound that is echoed off other fish and water species, allowing it to identify prey."

**Sound Production:**
Rather than continuous clicks, "The Ganges river dolphin most typically makes echolocation sounds such as clicks, bursts, and twitters." It can produce whistles but "rarely does so, suggesting that the whistle is a spontaneous sound and not a form of communication."

**Frequency Range:**
"Both species regularly produce frequencies lower than 15 kHz and the maximum frequency is thought to fall between 15 and 60 kHz."

**References:**
These details come from references [18], [19], and [21] in the article, citing Herald et al. (1969) and Mizue et al. (1971) for acoustic characteristics.","durationMs":4029,"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges_river_dolphin"}

input: {"url":"https://slashfilm.com/975697/why-clint-eastwood-always-tries-to-use-the-first-take-as-a-director","prompt":"What does Eastwood say/do about takes and economy? Is this about shooting or about brevity of film content?"}
result: {"bytes":63403,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Clint Eastwood's Approach to Takes

Eastwood employs an economical shooting strategy rather than focusing on film brevity. His philosophy centers on **limiting takes during production**.

## His Core Practice

Eastwood prioritizes capturing scenes on the first take whenever possible. He explained: *"The objective is to make everything sound like the first time it's said, so the only thing I can do is try to pick it up the very first time it is said."*

## The Reasoning

This approach serves multiple purposes:

1. **Authenticity**: He wants dialogue to sound natural and unrehearsed, mimicking real conversation
2. **Actor Performance**: Eastwood finds that constraining takes actually encourages compelling performances from skilled performers
3. **Set Efficiency**: He maintains a relaxed atmosphere with minimal tension, allowing crews to work quickly

## When Multiple Takes Occur

He only requests additional takes for technical or rhythmic reasons: *"Sometimes the rhythm or the timing isn't right, so you say let's do it again with a little more tempo"*—never for motivational re-direction or performance overhauls.

This stands in stark contrast to Stanley Kubrick's methodology of demanding 50-60 takes per scene. Eastwood's streamlined process has enabled his prolific career with 39 directing credits.","durationMs":4166,"url":"https://slashfilm.com/975697/why-clint-eastwood-always-tries-to-use-the-first-take-as-a-director"}

result: {"bytes":118935,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Saṃskāra, Vāsanā, and Their Interconnections in Yoga Philosophy

## Core Relationship to Memory and Karma

According to the text, saṃskāras are latent impressions formed when mental experiences fade. The article states: "Any vṛtti leaves its copy on the citta before fading away." These impressions function as a psychological storage system—"like a sound is imprinted on a tape recorder, or an image on film."

The connection to memory is direct: "Memory consists of the retrieval of these saṃskāras; memories are the reactivation of the imprints of sense objects." Importantly, saṃskāras aren't merely passive: "these saṃskāras are not just passive imprints but vibrant latent impulses that can get activated under conducive circumstances."

## Karma Cycle Integration

Saṃskāras form part of an interconnected cycle: "There is thus a cycle of kleśas, vṛttis and saṃskāras." Actions produce reactions recorded as saṃskāras, which then activate future mental states, perpetuating the saṃsāra cycle. The text notes saṃskāras "account for such things as personality traits, habits, compulsive and addictive behaviors."

## Perception and Subconscious Elements

The text identifies saṃskāras from past lives as forming the subconscious: "The notion of the subconscious in Western psychology corresponds to other less retrievable saṃskāras, primarily from previous lives, which remain latent as subliminal impressions."

**Disputes:** The text presents no significant disputes on these interconnections among traditional commentators.","durationMs":5508,"url":"https://iep.utm.edu/yoga/"}

result: {"bytes":190387,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Solon's Actions and Reforms

## What Solon Actually Did

According to the article, Solon's reforms had two main documented elements:

1. **Ended debt slavery**: He eliminated the practice of selling people into servitude for unpaid debts.

2. **Abolished the hektemoroi system**: He removed a serfdom arrangement where farmers were forced to surrender one-sixth of their harvest to local landowners.

Solon also implemented constitutional reforms, including "writing the laws in a place where people could read them," making legal codes publicly accessible.

## What Is Uncertain or Disputed

The article emphasizes significant uncertainty about the reforms' details. Ancient sources discussing "general debt cancellation" and "limits on personal wealth" are "today viewed as unlikely." The author explicitly warns: "Don't believe anyone who claims to know exactly what was involved."

## Solon's Own Poetry

Solon composed poems about his political work that the article describes as resembling "the 6th-century equivalent of tweets." These fragments, quoted by later authors, functioned to "set the public narrative for what he had done."

## Unanswered Questions

Scholars remain uncertain about the term "Seisachtheia" itself—whether it was contemporary terminology or invented later—and exactly how Solon persuaded the wealthy to accept these changes.","durationMs":5207,"url":"https://antigonejournal.com/2022/01/solon-seisachtheia/"}

result: {"bytes":1412416,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Sima Qian's Historical Method: Arguments and Disputes

## Core Argument

Michael Nylan proposes a "religious reading" of the *Shiji*, arguing that Sima Qian composed his history not primarily as an objective factual record, but as a pious act fulfilling filial duty. By commemorating "remarkable men and women from the Central States," Sima Qian sought to honor his father's dying wish while hoping that "potent spirits among the civilized dead would choose...to confer benefits" on his family as long as readers engaged with the text.

## Scholarly Disputes

**On Historical Objectivity:**
Nylan challenges the "standard readings" that emphasize Sima Qian's "rationalistic spirit" and objective methodology. Traditional scholars credited him as a careful, scrupulous historian who sifted through contradictory accounts. However, Nylan argues this interpretation is "anachronistic for the period" and misses the text's religious dimensions.

**On Authorial Motivation:**
Disagreement exists over whether Sima Qian prioritized individual genius, historical accuracy, or spiritual concerns. Some scholars view him as a romantic figure caught between cultural traditions; others emphasize his pragmatic compilation of ancestor records as a "family affair."

**On Content and Inclusion:**
The *Shiji*'s unusual focus on diverse social figures rather than political elites reflects its underlying religious purpose of commemorating the dead rather than establishing political authority.","durationMs":5649,"url":"https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/early-china/article/abs/sima-qian-a-true-historian/EE17A46DADC6E5FF949C8F8C549D824C"}

result: {"query":"Tadoma method history Sophia Alcorn Perkins Tad Chapman Oma Simpson 1920s Alcorn Hall Hall Inis","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_01JWndvG9S3rQTd8spMaXkh6","content":[{"title":"Sophia Alcorn","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Alcorn"},{"title":"Tadoma","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadoma"},{"title":"Alcorn Homestead","url":"https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/560"},{"title":"Perkins School","url":"https://00-73739769.nhdwebcentral.org/PerkinsSchool"},{"title":"www.wikipedia.org","url":"https://Www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadoma"},{"title":"encycloreader.org","url":"https://encycloreader.org/r/wikipedia.php?q=Tadoma"},{"title":"LLMpediaThe first transparent, open encyclopedia generated by LLMs","url":"https://llmpedia.scads.ai/deepseek/Tadoma.html"},{"title":"Tadoma Method:","url":"https://lifeprint.com/asl101/topics/tadoma.htm"},{"title":"Women’s History Month: KSD teacher developed method for Deafblind students to learn to speak","url":"https://www.amnews.com/?p=75423"},{"title":"www.perkins.org","url":"https://www.perkins.org/deafblind/"}]},"Based on the search results, here's information about the Tadoma method and the key figures you mentioned:

## The Tadoma Method History

The Tadoma method was invented by American teacher Sophie Alcorn and developed at the Perkins School for the Blind in Massachusetts. It is named after the first two children to whom it was taught: Winthrop "Tad" Chapman and Oma Simpson.

## Development and Timeline

Alcorn taught at the Kentucky School for the Deaf from 1909 to 1920, and it was here that she first developed the Tadoma method. In November 1910 the eight-year-old Oma Simpson came to the school. Oma had been deaf since birth and meningitis at age two had left her totally blind. Alcorn invented a system of touch on the cheek and neck to allow the child to imitate how to speak words.

## Later Development at Perkins

The Tadoma Method, named for Tad Chapman and Oma Simpson, was created by Alcorn in the 1920s at the Perkins School for the Blind in Massachusetts. Sophia K. Alcorn of Kentucky developed a method to teach oral speech to people who were deafblind, and Inis Hall introduced it at Perkins.

## Purpose and Impact

It was hoped that the students would learn to speak by trying to reproduce what they felt on the speaker's face and throat while touching their own face. Tadoma was the primary method of teaching speech and language to children who were deafblind until the early 1950s."],"durationSeconds":6.553037291999907,"searchCount":1}

Here are the search results:

## Jean Gebser and The Ever-Present Origin

Jean Gebser (1905-1973), a German-Swiss philosopher, poet, and cultural historian, created The Ever-Present Origin (Ursprung und Gegenwart), offering a visionary framework for understanding human consciousness throughout history.

## Core Concepts: Structures of Consciousness

Gebser identified five primary structures—archaic, magic, mythical, mental, and integral—which represent distinct ways of experiencing reality. These are discontinuous mutations rather than rungs in a linear ladder; each remains operative within contemporary consciousness and may function efficiently or deteriorate into a deficient form.

## Aperspectival Structure and Diaphaneity

The integral structure's "aperspectival" consciousness overcomes the limitations of duality, offering a holistic, multidimensional awareness that unites the past, present, and future. The integral structure, which Gebser also called the aperspectival structure of consciousness, is a transparent lucidity capable of seeing through all dimensionalities and time forms. The concept of transparency (diaphaneity) is a keyword for the integral structure.

## The Mutation to Integral Consciousness

At present humanity is undergoing a mutation from the mental, perspectival structure of consciousness to the integral, aperspectival structure.

(1968), 195, pp. 215-243 215 With 3 plates and 14 text-figures","url":"https://www.cns.nyu.edu/~tony/vns/readings/hubel-wiesel-1968.pdf"},{"title":"Simple cell","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_cell"},{"title":"Geometroneurodynamics","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/quant-ph/0311110"},{"title":"Direction and speed selectivity properties for spatio-temporal receptive fields according to the generalized Gaussian derivative model for visual receptive fields","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.08101"}]},"I've retrieved search results on Hubel and Wiesel's groundbreaking work on receptive fields in the striate cortex. Here's what the results show:

## Key Findings

**Landmark Papers (1959-1962):**
Hubel and Wiesel published "Receptive fields of single neurones in the cat's striate cortex" in 1959, and followed this with "Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat's visual cortex" in 1962.

**Discovery of Orientation Selectivity:**
Hubel and Wiesel identified orientation-selective cells in the cat's visual cortex and generated a map of the receptive field of cortical cells. They noticed that rectangular bars of light were more effective stimuli than circular spots of light, as long as the orientation was adjusted to the correct angle appropriate for each cell.

**Simple and Complex Cells:**
Hubel and Wiesel classified cortical receptive fields into two main categories – simple cells and complex cells. According to their model, simple receptive fields are constructed from the convergence of geniculate inputs with receptive fields aligned in visual space, while complex receptive fields originate from the convergence of simple cells with similar orientation preferences.

result: {"query":"Polanyi tacit knowing "we can know more than we can tell" Stanford Encyclopedia OR Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy Personal Knowledge","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_01Bc71kZjTX62vLLJXRdTaXq","content":[{"title":"Commentary on Knowing More Than We Can Tell","url":"https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-00742-2_57"},{"title":"Polanyi%27s paradox","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polanyi%27s_paradox"},{"title":"Tim Thornton - Polanyi","url":"https://sites.google.com/site/drtimthornton/courses/tacit-knowledge/polanyi"},{"title":"Tacit knowledge","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacit_knowledge"},{"title":"Profiles in Knowledge: 5 Important 20th Century Philosophers — Polanyi, Popper, Lonergan, Lakatos, Kuhn","url":"https://stangarfield.medium.com/profiles-in-knowledge-5-important-20th-century-philosophers-polanyi-popper-lonergan-lakatos-3bb12b16a3bf"},{"title":"Gems from Polanyi's Personal Knowledge and Tacit Dimension","url":"https://extendedbrain.substack.com/p/gems-from-polanyis-personal-knowledge"},{"title":"The Tacit Dimension by Michael Polanyi","url":"https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/225665"},{"title":"Knowledge, tacit - Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy","url":"https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/knowledge-tacit/v-1"},{"title":"Polanyi’s Paradox","url":"https://encyclopedia.pub/entry/32479"},{"title":"The Tacit Dimension [Excerpt]","url":"https://tacit-knowledge-architecture.com/object/the-tacit-dimension-excerpt/"}]},"I've found comprehensive information about Polanyi's tacit knowing and the famous phrase "we can know more than we can tell." Here are the key results:

## Overview

The term tacit knowing is attributed to Michael Polanyi's *Personal Knowledge* (1958), and in his later work *The Tacit Dimension* (1966), Polanyi made the assertion that "we can know more than we can tell."

## The Core Concept

Polanyi states not only that there is knowledge that cannot be adequately articulated by verbal means, but also that all knowledge is rooted in tacit knowledge. Summarised in the slogan "We can know more than we can tell", Polanyi's paradox is mainly to explain the cognitive phenomenon that there exist many tasks which we, human beings, understand intuitively how to perform but cannot verbalize the rules or procedures behind it.

## Examples and Applications

When we know something, we recognize wholes, not particulars: we absorb the particulars. For instance, we can easily recognize a face, but cannot usually tell what in particular distinguishes it from other faces.

## Philosophical Context

The term derives from the work of Michael Polanyi (1891–1976) whose critique of positivistic philosophy of science grew into a fully developed theory of knowledge. Polanyi believed that the 'scientific' account of knowledge as a fully explicit formalizable body of statements did not allow for an adequate account of discovery and growth.

result: {"bytes":75297,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Indian Aesthetic Theory: Rasa in the Nāṭya Śāstra

## Core Concept

The earliest Indian aesthetic text, Bharata's *Nāṭya Śāstra* (c. 300 CE), introduces *rasa*—literally meaning "taste"—as central to dramatic experience. Bharata explains that just as connoisseurs savor food prepared with multiple condiments, learned viewers relish stable emotions when actors manifest them through transitory emotions and various performance registers.

## Key Characteristics

**What Rasa Is:**
The term operates as both gustatory sensation and aesthetic experience. *Rasa* represents the emotional savoring that audiences derive from drama, distinct from ordinary emotion. It emerges from combining multiple elements—emotions, reactions, and performance techniques—much like spices combine to create complex flavors.

## Interpretive Disputes

Indian philosophers disagreed about *rasa's* location: whether it resides in the actor, audience, character, author, or the work itself. Despite this disagreement, all recognized that pleasure and relishing constitute the aesthetic experience.

## Broader Significance

This theory positions food preparation as a legitimate art form worthy of serious philosophical consideration, contrasting sharply with Western aesthetic traditions that often dismiss culinary pleasure as lesser than other arts.","durationMs":4962,"url":"https://indianphilosophyblog.org/2017/08/20/the-indian-theory-of-taste/"}

result: {"bytes":187316,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Warren and Brandeis (1890) and "The Right to Privacy"

## The Core Contribution

Warren and Brandeis's foundational essay introduced the concept of privacy as a distinct legal right, grounded in protecting "the right to be let alone." They argued this principle was already implicit in common law but required explicit recognition given new technological threats like photography and invasive press coverage.

## Key Theoretical Foundations

Rather than focusing on property or intellectual creations, Warren and Brandeis emphasized what they called the "inviolate personality"—the protection of a person's thoughts, sentiments, and emotions from public dissemination. They framed privacy as protecting "peace of mind" and personal dignity.

## Major Scholarly Disputes

**Prosser's Systematization**: Legal scholar William Prosser (1960) identified four distinct privacy interests emerging from tort law: intrusion into seclusion, public disclosure of embarrassing facts, false light publicity, and appropriation of likeness.

**Reductionist Critique**: Judith Thomson (1975) argued privacy claims reduce to violations of other rights (property, bodily security) rather than constituting a unified interest. Thomson claimed privacy was merely a "cluster" of disparate rights.

**Competing Interpretations**: Scholars debated whether Warren and Brandeis grounded privacy in property rights or in a broader principle of personal inviolability—fundamentally shaping how subsequent theorists conceptualized privacy's foundation.","durationMs":4199,"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/privacy/"}

Here are the key findings from the search results:

## Sentinel Behavior and the Watchman's Song

The sentinel system minimizes the foraging-vigilance trade-off by having one individual on raised guard scanning the environment for predators, while the rest of the group forages. In species where individuals cannot visually check for a sentinel without interrupting foraging, sentinels typically give soft calls called the "Watchman's song".

## Meerkat Sentinel Calls

In contrast to many other species with sentinel calls, meerkats have not only one, but six different sentinel call types. These call types include single-note, double-note, triple-note, multiple-note, di-drrr and wheek calls, with single and double-note calls acting as 'all-clear' signals referred to as sentinel calming calls.

## Foragers' Response to Sentinel Presence

Surveillance calls provide key information about sentinel presence, satiation level and height, allowing receivers to optimize their foraging. Foraging group members adjust their vigilance behavior in response to playbacks of sentinel calls depending on the identity and experience of the caller.

The research involves collaboration with Professor Marta Manser, whose work is prominently featured in these studies on meerkat communication and sentinel behavior."],"durationSeconds":6.029640417000278,"searchCount":1}

Here are the key findings:

## The Discovery

While working on "The Conversation" starring Gene Hackman, legendary editor Walter Murch noticed that every time he made a cut, it seemed to line up perfectly with Gene Hackman blinking.

## The Theory: Cut as Blink

Murch suggests starting a conversation with somebody and watching when they blink, noting "I believe you will find that your listener will blink at the precise moment he or she 'gets' the idea of what you are saying."

Blinking seems to be a way for us to "process" chunks of reality, allowing our minds to take in whole moments rather than one continuous stream of information. Blinks are like punctuation marks that turn a ramble of thoughts into understandable sentences.

Murch suggests that cutting works the exact same way, where "a shot presents us with an idea, or a sequence of ideas, and the cut is a 'blink' that separates and punctuates those ideas."

## The Book

In 1995, Murch published a book on film editing, "In the Blink of an Eye: A Perspective on Film Editing," in which he urges editors to prioritise emotion.

The book emphasizes paying attention to when actors blink, noting that a good actor's blinks will be tied to his/her thoughts and emotions, and Murch noticed with Gene Hackman that where Hackman blinked was often a good place to cut a sequence."],"durationSeconds":6.968780791999772,"searchCount":1}

result: {"bytes":112235,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Nāgārjuna on Causation and Conditions

Based on the encyclopedia entry, Nāgārjuna systematically refutes four possible causal relationships:

## The Four Alternatives

Nāgārjuna examines whether things could be produced from: (1) themselves, (2) other things, (3) both themselves and others, or (4) neither. He argues that none of these alternatives allows cause and effect to exist with *svabhāva* (inherent existence).

## Key Arguments

**Mutual Dependence**: Nāgārjuna establishes that cause and effect are mutually dependent rather than independently substantial. As the text states: "the effect depends *existentially* on the cause...and the cause depends at least *notionally* on the effect."

**Conceptual Construction**: He argues that causal relations themselves are conceptually constructed. The "causal field" (cause plus background conditions) only coheres through our cognitive act of assembling it for explanatory purposes.

## Regarding Hypothetical Form

The entry does not explicitly discuss whether Nāgārjuna employs a hypothetical ground/consequence logical form. However, his method involves systematizing alternatives and eliminating each through logical analysis, which structurally resembles conditional reasoning, though the text doesn't label it as such.

The broader point: causation cannot ground *svabhāva*, since causally related objects depend on conceptualization and therefore lack intrinsic existence.","durationMs":4440,"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/nagarjuna/"}

## Overview

The Protection of Information in Computer Systems is a 1975 seminal publication by Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder about information security. The paper describes desired functions, design principles, and examples of elementary protection and authentication mechanisms.

## The Design Principles

The principles include: Economy of mechanism (simple and small designs), Fail-safe defaults (lack of access by default), Complete mediation (control access to every object), Open design (security by obscurity does not work), Separation of privilege (require two keys when possible), Least privilege (operate using the least set of privileges necessary), and Least common mechanism (minimize shared mechanisms).

## Scholarly Reception and Critique

In the following decades, these principles were used occasionally as guidelines for developing secure systems, found their way into the DoD's Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria, and were highlighted in security textbooks.

Richard E. Smith published "A Contemporary Look at Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 Design Principles" in IEEE Security & Privacy in November-December 2012, which represents a retrospective critique examining the limitations and applicability of these foundational principles to modern security challenges."],"durationSeconds":6.106251083999872,"searchCount":1}

## Key Findings:

**First Use of "Plagiarius" for Literary Theft:**
Martial is the first classical poet to use the term plagiarius to refer to literary theft in Epigram 1.52.

**The Fidentinus Connection:**
Epigram 1.52 is part of the "Fidentinus cycle," or the series of six epigrams (Ep. 1.29, 38, 52, 53, 66, and 72) that deal with the plagiarist Fidentinus. Martial asserts that Fidentinus has mixed his own poem into a libellus that otherwise contains Martial's epigrams, and has attempted to pass the entire volume off as his own.

**Etymology: From Kidnapper to Literary Thief:**
In the 1st century, the use of the Latin word plagiarius (literally "kidnapper") to denote copying someone else's creative work was pioneered by the Roman poet Martial, who complained that another poet had "kidnapped his verses". 

The term previously had meant "kidnap" and it specifically related to either the kidnapping of one's slaves or to take a free person and make them into a slave. input: {"url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3616034/","prompt":"Summarize how Ganges river dolphins echolocate: click behavior, range, whether click rate adapts with distance, source level. Anything about interpreting absence of echoes? Short paraphrase."}
result: {"bytes":252075,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Ganges River Dolphin Echolocation Summary

**Click Characteristics:**
Ganges river dolphins produce "broadband transients" with surprisingly low frequency. Their centroid frequency averages 61.4 kHz—"almost an octave lower than expected from their size." Clicks last approximately 21.7 microseconds.

**Range & Click Rate:**
These animals employ high-repetition echolocation, with an interclick interval averaging 35 milliseconds across entire click series. This elevated click rate suggests "searching for prey within a shorter range than most other studied odontocetes," indicating adaptation to close-range foraging in shallow rivers.

**Source Level:**
Ganges dolphins produce notably low source levels, averaging 183.3 dB (peak-to-peak), which is "1–2 orders of magnitude lower than those of similar sized marine delphinids." This reduced amplitude likely reflects adaptation to acoustically complex, shallow freshwater habitats with high reverberation.

**Echo Interpretation:**
The paper doesn't explicitly address how these dolphins interpret absent echoes or process ambiguous acoustic information—only that their low source levels and high click rates reflect constraints imposed by shallow, cluttered river environments rather than optimization for long-range detection.","durationMs":4458,"url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3616034/"}

result: {"query":"Brandeis Olmstead dissent "right to be let alone" Cooley 1880 Treatise on Torts origin of phrase Warren Brandeis law review","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_01KG31AhvcTKStLKQKUFRX9t","content":[{"title":"journals.librarypublishing.arizona.edu","url":"https://journals.librarypublishing.arizona.edu/arizlrev/article/9025/galley/8248/download"},{"title":"harvard  law review","url":"https://faculty.uml.edu/sgallagher/harvard__law_review.htm"},{"title":"digital.ub.uni-potsdam.de","url":"https://digital.ub.uni-potsdam.de/content/pagetext/328950"},{"title":"Artigo Destaque dos editores","url":"https://jus.com.br/artigos/57228/o-surgimento-e-o-desenvolvimento-do-right-to-privacy-nos-estados-unidos"},{"title":"sdhumanities.org","url":"https://sdhumanities.org/tag/constitution/page/83/"},{"title":"revista.trf3.jus.br","url":"https://revista.trf3.jus.br/index.php/rtrf3/article/download/468/440/998"},{"title":"sdhumanities.org","url":"https://sdhumanities.org/tag/2023/page/9/"},{"title":"1928 June 4","url":"https://todayinclh.com/?p=6545"},{"title":"OP1NS 0005","url":"https://pdf.online.salempress.com/OP1NS_0005.pdf"}]},"Based on the search results, here's what I found about the relationship between these key legal concepts:

## Origin of the Phrase

Thomas Cooley coined the phrase "the right to be let alone" in his Treatise on the Law of Torts (1st ed. 1879), where he wrote: "Personal immunity--the right of one's person may be said to be a right of complete immunity; the right to be alone."

## Warren and Brandeis Law Review Article

Louis Brandeis and Samuel Warren published the first-ever article on "The Right to Privacy" in the Harvard Law Review on December 15, 1890. Warren and Brandeis were careful to credit Cooley with this creation and cited the second edition of the treatise.

## Brandeis's Olmstead Dissent

In his famous dissent in Olmstead v. United States (1928), Brandeis defined the "right to be let alone" as "the most comprehensive of rights, and the right most valued by civilized men."

The phrase thus traveled from Cooley's 1880 treatise on tort law through the influential Warren-Brandeis 1890 Harvard Law Review article and finally into Brandeis's landmark 1928 Supreme Court dissent, becoming a foundational concept in American privacy jurisprudence."],"durationSeconds":5.238606166999787,"searchCount":1}

result: {"query":"túngara frog males add chucks when competing males calling chorus size; female choice with competing calls","results":[{"tool_use_id":"srvtoolu_012rMWH7fQ5UEDLan8sjNbBw","content":[{"title":"par.nsf.gov","url":"https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10554926"},{"title":"Published January 10, 2023 | Version v1","url":"https://zenodo.org/record/7521631"},{"title":"www.arxiv.org","url":"https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/1610.03930"},{"title":"Social Science","url":"https://scienceline.org/2011/03/the-chuck-heard-round-the-world/"},{"title":"frogs mating call also attracts predators 180949463","url":"https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/frogs-mating-call-also-attracts-predators-180949463/?no-ist"},{"title":"stricollections.org","url":"https://stricollections.org/stri/taxa/index.php?tid=11229"},{"title":"Volume 121, Issue 8 pp. 749-759","url":"https://onlinelibrary-wiley-com-443.webvpn.zafu.edu.cn/doi/abs/10.1111/eth.12387"},{"title":"Modeling sexual selection in Túngara frog and rationality of mate choice","url":"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1610.03930"},{"title":"Physalaemus pustulosus","url":"https://bio.acousti.ca/ja/node/57556"}]},"Based on the search results, here's what research has revealed about túngara frog males adding chucks in response to competing calls and female choice:

## Chorus Competition and Chuck Addition

As chorus size increased, calls increasingly had their chucks overlapped by the high-amplitude beginning part of other callers' whines, and playback experiments revealed such overlap reduced the attractiveness of calls to females, but that appending additional chucks mitigated this effect.

## Female Preference for Complex Calls

Females are five times more likely to choose a synthetic whine-chuck over a simple whine. Males start to be daring and chuck when they have to compete for females, and when they do, males can add up to seven chucks, but they rarely go for more than three.

## Male Strategic Response to Chorus Size

Interestingly, if there are only a few males in the pond they don't chuck, because there are enough females to go around, so they don't have to out-sexy each other, but it's only when males have to compete for females that they start to be daring.

## Call Complexity Components

When chorusing, túngara frog calls consist of a whine typically followed by 1–3 chucks. The research shows that this dynamic adjustment of call complexity in response to competition creates an emergent pattern where female preferences for more elaborate signals appear to drive the evolution of more complex calling strategies."],"durationSeconds":6.543856124999001,"searchCount":1}

// true of then. Nothing here is ever "corrected" by deletion.
export const BELIEF_KIND = "competency-philosophy";

/**
 * recordBelief(ex, { statement, basis, evidence, giver }) → appended entry.
 *   statement  the claim itself, plain language
 *   basis      what measured event grounds it (a real run's numbers, never
 *              "it seems like")
 *   evidence   optional structured data (e.g. a run's instances/population/
 *              activation) so the claim is checkable against what produced it
 *   giver      "archon:polanyi" for a standing philosophical position this
 *              archon holds; "mechanical:<fn>" for a note auto-derived from
 *              one run's own numbers (learn-pass.js's beliefFromRun) — kept
 *              distinct so a reader can tell reflection from raw derivation
 */
export function recordBelief(ex, { statement, basis, evidence = null, giver = "archon:polanyi" } = {}) {
  if (!statement) throw new TypeError("recordBelief: statement is declared");
  const seq = ex.ledger.lines.filter((l) => l.kind === BELIEF_KIND && l.role === "belief").length + 1;
  const line = appendLedgerLine(ex.ledger, {
    role: "belief", kind: BELIEF_KIND,
 * demonstrateExpertise(ex, name, { draw, model, base }) → { line, baseline,
 *   shaped, baselineScore, shapedScore, delta }
 *
 * THE PROOF the user asked for: "genuinely recording the activity so we can
 * prove that competency was learned by a local model in this way." The
 * SHAPE is never learned by the model — learnParadigmEmergent/learnForm are
 * pure measurement, recorded above under a mechanical giver, not Polanyi's
 * or any model's. What a model CAN be shown to do is write BETTER once
 * handed that measured shape as information (Gary: information, never a
 * rule to imitate in language — "model is just the mouth"): `draw` is
 * called TWICE with the SAME open ask, once bare, once with the current
 * expertise's own lines (facts, not instructions) appended.
 *
 * `base` (optional): a real, UNCHOSEN piece of material to write FROM — the
 * user: "have it try to generate something in that modality based on a
 * random Wikipedia article… so there is a base to draw from." When given
 * (wiki-base.js's fetchWikipediaBase result: { url, title, text }), BOTH
 * asks require the reply to draw its content from that material, so a good
 * score cannot come from reciting a memorized stock example — the model
 * must produce genuinely NOVEL content in the modality. Its provenance
 * (url + sha256) is stored on the ledger line, honestly, as what the model
 * actually wrote from. Without `base`, the ask is the old open form ask.
 *
 * Both replies, both prompts, the model's name, the base's provenance if
 * any, and both scores — recomputable by scoreAgainstExpertise on the
 * stored text alone — are appended to the SAME ledger as a "demonstration"
 * line, given by the model itself, never by Polanyi: this line is the
 * model's own output, not the engine's measurement.
 */
export async function demonstrateExpertise(ex, name, { draw, model = "unknown", maxTokens = 260, base = null } = {}) {
  if (typeof draw !== "function") throw new TypeError("demonstrateExpertise: draw (the local model's own call) is declared");
  const cur = projectExpertise(ex, name);
  if (!cur) throw new TypeError(`demonstrateExpertise: "${name}" has never been learned — nothing to demonstrate against`);","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}

result: {"bytes":172844,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Koestler's Holon Theory and Gould's Critique

## Koestler's Claim

Koestler argues that reality organizes itself into hierarchies ("holarchies") where each unit ("holon") functions as both an autonomous entity and a component of larger systems. He uses the Janus metaphor: each holon has "a face turned toward the higher levels" as a subordinate part, and "a face turned toward the lower levels" as a quasi-autonomous whole.

## Gould's Main Criticisms

Gould acknowledges the theory's appeal but finds Koestler's *specific applications* unconvincing. The reviewer criticizes Koestler's particular claims about evolution and human neurobiology rather than rejecting the hierarchy concept outright.

## Scientific Support Question

Gould does **not** declare holon theory scientifically unsupported generally. Instead, he argues that Koestler misapplies it—particularly when claiming humans are "evolutionary misfits" due to improper brain integration. Gould contends hierarchy is "not a mechanism" without explaining *why* organisms behave differently.

## Claim About Causation Direction

The article contains **no mention** of any principle stating "low sets possibility for high, high sets probability for low." Gould focuses on Koestler's faulty factual claims about evolution and brain structure, not on any bidirectional causation principle.","durationMs":4842,"url":"https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1978/04/20/koestlers-solution/"}

result: {"bytes":44628,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Xu Shen's Scholarly Agenda

**Author:** Timothy O'Neill  
**Year:** 2013

**Article's Central Argument:**

O'Neill contends that Xu Shen designed the *Shuowen jiezi*'s structure to demonstrate that "changes in the writing systems are historically and graphemically observable." His overarching thesis is that this lexicographic method allows scholars to recover the original intentions of ancient sages by tracing writing system reforms backwards to understand how classical texts were originally written and words classified in the ancient *guwen* script.

Essentially, O'Neill argues Xu Shen's scholarly agenda was creating a tool for textual philology—one that would make classical authorial intent recoverable through systematic analysis of graphemic evolution.","durationMs":3362,"url":"https://lockwoodonlinejournals.com/index.php/jaos/article/view/1862"}

result: {"bytes":44257,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Research Summary: Emotional Arcs in Stories

## Key Findings

The researchers analyzed 1,327 fiction texts from Project Gutenberg using natural language processing to identify emotional patterns. They discovered that complex stories are built from "a set of six core emotional arcs which form the essential building blocks of complex emotional trajectories."

## Methodology

The team employed multiple analytical approaches—matrix decomposition, supervised learning, and unsupervised learning—to classify emotional trajectories throughout narratives. They measured success by correlating emotional arc types with download frequency.

## Vonnegut Connection

**Notable omission:** The provided abstract does not mention Kurt Vonnegut or reference his well-known proposal about story shapes. While Vonnegut famously claimed most stories follow predictable emotional patterns, this abstract offers no explicit comparison to or validation of his framework.

## Key Quote

The researchers found that "particular emotional arcs enjoy greater success, as measured by downloads," suggesting certain narrative emotional patterns resonate more strongly with audiences than others.

The work represents a data-driven approach to understanding narrative structure through computational analysis rather than traditional literary theory.","durationMs":3470,"url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07772"}

result: {"bytes":247541,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Murch on Blinks and Cuts

**Blinks as Markers:**
Murch observes that listeners blink precisely when they "get" an idea during conversation. Blinks function as punctuation, breaking continuous information into digestible moments.

**Cuts Mirror Blinks:**
In film, cuts serve an identical purpose. As Murch explains, "the cut is a 'blink' that separates and punctuates those ideas." Both separate concepts into coherent, consumable units—creating narrative sentences from raw footage.

**Audience Synchronization:**
When films work effectively, viewers' blinking patterns synchronize with each other and the film's rhythm. This collective experience suggests audiences unconsciously align with well-edited content, whereas scattered editing causes audiences to psychologically withdraw.

**Cutting Rhythm Guidelines:**
Murch identifies statistical parallels between natural blinking rates and film cutting frequencies. Action sequences might average 25 cuts per minute, while dialogue scenes typically hover around 6 cuts per minute for comfortable viewing in American cinema.

The core insight: editing succeeds because cuts mirror how our brains naturally process reality through blinks.","durationMs":4307,"url":"https://musicbed.com/blog/filmmaking/editing/editing-secrets-from-legendary-editor-walter-murch"}

result: {"bytes":1042594,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Royal Yorùbá Bards (Arókin): Craft and Historical Practice

## Their Craft

The Arókin were court musicians and historical specialists who employed music and poetic recitation as their primary medium. They performed with instruments including the aro (iron rings) and ṣèkèrè (beaded rattle), using these to accompany their historical narratives.

## Recitation: Adaptive Rather Than Fixed

The article suggests the Arókin's approach was fundamentally adaptive. They deployed historical precedent flexibly, incorporating new information and adjusting narratives to suit present circumstances. The author notes their tradition involved "assimilating events" to explain current meanings rather than maintaining rigid, unchanging accounts.

## View of History

Notably, the Arókin prioritized consolation (itùnû) over documentation. Their primary historical function was "to cool down his personal grief"—specifically the ruler's emotional distress following losses. 

Beyond providing mere etiology or political legitimation, they emphasized "the restoration of equanimity against grief and anger." History served an emotional and psychological purpose: making sense of present suffering through reference to the past, or adopting new interpretive frameworks when traditional ones proved insufficient.

This reveals a conception of history fundamentally oriented toward managing personal and collective emotions rather than establishing factual chronicles.","durationMs":5262,"url":"https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/history-in-africa/article/history-and-consolation-royal-yoruba-bards-comment-on-their-craft/32D824B3623903506ED42F8599D22EFF"}

result: {"bytes":244322,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Polanyi on Tacit Knowing

## Core Concept

Polanyi emphasizes that "we know more than we can tell," suggesting knowledge exceeds what can be explicitly articulated. He frames tacit knowing as an active, practical process rather than passive knowledge possession.

## Key Characteristics

**Personal Knowledge**: Polanyi describes knowing as "active comprehension of things known, an action that requires skill." This integrates theoretical and practical dimensions—even acquiring abstract knowledge demands intellectual skill.

**Balance of Objectivity/Subjectivity**: Rather than eliminating the knower from knowledge (pure objectivity), Polanyi argues the knower's characteristics remain inherent to understanding.

## Proximal/Distal Distinction

Polanyi distinguishes between:
- **Proximal**: the particulars we attend from (often tacitly)
- **Distal**: the focal object we attend to

We grasp wholes through subsidiary awareness of parts without explicitly articulating those parts.

## Explicability Question

The webpage notes Polanyi himself admits difficulty defining exactly what "tacit" means. Tacit knowledge represents what remains *implicit*—not necessarily impossible to articulate, but what we successfully employ without explicit formulation.

## Criticisms

Collins later challenged Polanyi's framework, questioning whether tacit knowledge can be meaningfully distinguished from explicit knowledge or whether the boundary remains unclear.","durationMs":4299,"url":"https://sites.google.com/site/drtimthornton/courses/tacit-knowledge/polanyi"}

“‘So far so good,’ said she, when I had ended my story, ‘and now pay
attention to what I am about to tell you—heaven itself, indeed, will
recall it to your recollection. First you will come to the Sirens who
enchant all who come near them. If any one unwarily draws in too close
and hears the singing of the Sirens, his wife and children will never
welcome him home again, for they sit in a green field and warble him to
death with the sweetness of their song. There is a great heap of dead
men’s bones lying all around, with the flesh still rotting off them.
Therefore pass these Sirens by, and stop your men’s ears with wax that
none of them may hear; but if you like you can listen yourself, for you
may get the men to bind you as you stand upright on a cross piece half
way up the mast,99 and they must lash the rope’s ends to the mast
itself, that you may have the pleasure of listening. If you beg and
pray the men to unloose you, then they must bind you faster.

“‘When your crew have taken you past these Sirens, I cannot give you
coherent directions100 as to which of two courses you are to take; I
will lay the two alternatives before you, and you must consider them
for yourself. On the one hand there are some overhanging rocks against
which the deep blue waves of Amphitrite beat with terrific fury; the
blessed gods call these rocks the Wanderers. Here not even a bird may
pass, no, not even the timid doves that bring ambrosia to Father Jove,
but the sheer rock always carries off one of them, and Father Jove has
to send another to make up their number; no ship that ever yet came to
earshot of the land, and the ship was going at a good rate, the Sirens
saw that we were getting in shore and began with their singing.

“‘Come here,’ they sang, ‘renowned Ulysses, honour to the Achaean name,
and listen to our two voices. No one ever sailed past us without
staying to hear the enchanting sweetness of our song—and he who listens
will go on his way not only charmed, but wiser, for we know all the
ills that the gods laid upon the Argives and Trojans before Troy, and
can tell you everything that is going to happen over the whole world.’

“They sang these words most musically, and as I longed to hear them
further I made signs by frowning to my men that they should set me
free; but they quickened their stroke, and Eurylochus and Perimedes
bound me with still stronger bonds till we had got out of hearing of
the Sirens’ voices. Then my men took the wax from their ears and
unbound me.

“Immediately after we had got past the island I saw a great wave from
which spray was rising, and I heard a loud roaring sound. The men were
so frightened that they loosed hold of their oars, for the whole sea
resounded with the rushing of the waters,103 but the ship stayed where
it was, for the men had left off rowing. I went round, therefore, and
exhorted them man by man not to lose heart.

“‘My friends,’ said I, ‘this is not the first time that we have been in

result: {"bytes":308002,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Brillat-Savarin's *Physiologie du goût*

**Genre & Structure**: Brillat-Savarin co-founded the gastronomic essay genre alongside Grimod de La Reynière. The work opens with twenty aphorisms on gastronomy, followed by "Gastronomical Meditations" covering thirty topics (taste, appetite, digestion, obesity, etc.), and concludes with "Miscellanea" containing anecdotes and memories.[1]

**Publication**: Published anonymously in December 1825, just two months before his death in February 1826, though the author's identity became widely known.[2]

**Core Philosophy**: Brillat-Savarin emphasized that "Animals feed: man eats: only the man of intellect knows how to eat," suggesting eating as an intellectual pursuit rather than mere sustenance.[3]

**Dietary Arguments**: He advocated low-carbohydrate eating, arguing that sugar and refined flour caused obesity. Instead, he promoted protein-rich foods: "carnivorous animals never grow fat" while those fed "potatoes, grain, or any kind of flour" fatten readily.[4]

text:
Four of the 12 batches are in: 2, 5, 7 and 12, which is 26 of the 82 dossiers. All have passed the checker, and none says "justified". The other eight batches are still running.

- **Fixed `snip.mjs`.** It imported `quotes.js` from the old `eoreader7/` path, which no longer exists, so nobody could cut a snip. It now imports from `khora/`. `snip.mjs check` runs again, but it reports some existing manifests (e.g. `whitman.json`) whose source file is missing. I haven't audited that list yet.
- **Hand-written manifests.** Agents wrote six `copyrighted_deferred` manifests by hand (meyer, shklovsky, mayeroff, ubuntu, ostrom, tschichold) while the tool was broken. They match the `defer` format, but I'll re-validate them with the fixed tool.
- **Stronger findings so far:**
  - **sockeye:** the verdict is "fails". The snip says nothing about homing, and the compendium's "pull grows as the fish nears home" isn't in the source.
  - **kleeneUp:** the verdict is "fails". The organ, the compendium and `kleenup.txt` each describe a different doctrine, and Kleene never argued the rule credited to him.
  - **abhinavagupta:** the compendium's "never a view from nowhere" nearly inverts his sadharanikarana (depersonalisation).
  - **ostrom:** the compendium points at `ethos.js`, which never mentions her.
  - **tschichold:** the compendium credits the 1928 book for a stance he later repudiated.
  - **brahmagupta:** the quoted rule is the addition rule, but our line matches the subtraction rule.
  - **tala:** in the verse we cite, "talas" means a cymbal class of instruments, not a rhythmic cycle.
- **Limits.** Almost no agent could read a primary book. Many findings rest on SEP entries, abstracts or search snippets, and several sites returned 403. I'll label those dossiers lower-confidence and spot-check the sharpest ones against the sources before changing any compendium text.

I'll apply the fixes once all 12 have reported.

Pullum's essay "50 Years of Stupid Grammar Advice" and his critique of Strunk and White's *Elements of Style*, particularly regarding passive voice:

## Overview of Pullum's Essay

In 2009, on the 50th anniversary of the publication of Strunk and White's *The Elements of Style*, Geoffrey K. Pullum wrote an essay for the Chronicle of Higher Education titled "50 Years of Stupid Grammar Advice."

## Pullum's Main Criticism

Pullum argues that *The Elements of Style* does not deserve the esteem in which it is held by American college graduates, that its advice ranges from limp platitudes to inconsistent nonsense, and that its enormous influence has significantly degraded American students' grasp of English grammar.

## Critique of Passive Voice Advice

Pullum spends a great deal of time debunking the myth perpetuated by Strunk and White that the passive voice is unacceptable. According to Pullum, the authors' attempt to discredit the passive voice is "either grammatically misguided or disingenuous," part of "the book's toxic mix of purism, atavism, and personal eccentricity."

## Pullum's Assessment of the Authors

Pullum describes both authors as grammatical incompetents, noting that Strunk had very little analytical understanding of syntax, and White had even less."],"durationSeconds":5.769425750000402,"searchCount":1}

input: {"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/levinas/","prompt":"How does Levinas characterize the face of the Other, ethics as first philosophy, and the relation to Buber's I-Thou (his critique of Buber)? Any mention of reciprocity/asymmetry? Short paraphrase only."}
result: {"bytes":255942,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Levinas on the Face, Ethics, and Alterity

**The Face as Expression:**
Levinas describes the face of the other as expressing vulnerability and defenselessness. The facial expression signifies passively: "Do not kill me," opposing our desire for mastery through what he calls "passive resistance." This encounter interrupts our freedom and summons us to responsibility.

**Ethics as First Philosophy:**
Rather than ontology or metaphysics, Levinas argues that "ethics that should be so conceived" as first philosophy. Ethics emerges not as theory but through the lived encounter with alterity, operating at a pre-cognitive level through embodied sensibility.

**Regarding Buber's I-Thou:**
The provided text does not contain discussion of Levinas' critique of Buber's I-Thou philosophy, so I cannot address that comparison based on this source.

**Asymmetry vs. Reciprocity:**
Levinas emphasizes radical asymmetry. Responsibility is not reciprocal; I am responsible for the other without requiring their reciprocal responsibility toward me. The relationship remains asymmetrical—the other's claim on me precedes any mutual exchange or contract.

This asymmetrical structure distinguishes Levinas from dialogical philosophies emphasizing mutual recognition.","durationMs":4547,"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/levinas/"}

input: {"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/buber/","prompt":"Summarize I-Thou vs I-It: is I-It bad or necessary, can Thou be a category/known in advance, reciprocity, and Levinas's critique. Short paraphrase."}
result: {"bytes":125749,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# I-Thou vs I-It: Core Distinctions

**Necessity vs. Badness of I-It:**
The I-It relationship isn't portrayed as inherently evil but rather as a reduced mode of engagement. Buber associates it with "subject-object relations" and instrumental thinking—the domain of science and practical knowledge. However, the text suggests this reduction becomes problematic only when it dominates human experience, excluding genuine encounters.

**The Thou as Pre-categorical:**
Critically, the Thou cannot be known in advance or treated as an abstract category. As the article states, "The I-Thou, which cannot be reduced to a concept" represents an actual experiential encounter rather than conceptual knowledge. This resists theoretical systematization.

**Reciprocity Questions:**
Reciprocity varies by sphere. Between humans, the I-Thou involves genuine mutuality, but Buber distinguishes this from other encounters—relations with nature remain "pre-dialogic" because they lack reciprocal response, while the divine relationship transcends conventional reciprocity.

**Levinas's Critique:**
Levinas objected that Buber remained trapped in "aestheticizing attitude" rather than embracing "ethics as first philosophy." Unlike Levinas's ethics, where the Other's demands impose excessive obligation, Buber's I-Thou emphasizes mutual encounter between equals, not asymmetrical ethical demand.","durationMs":4951,"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/buber/"}

Archives Husserl. seminaire Lectures levinassiennes 2025 2026","url":"https://paysgermaniques.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/2.BV_.DCL-Programme.-Archives-Husserl.-seminaire-Lectures-levinassiennes-2025-2026.pdf"},{"title":"projet eee.levinasPhF","url":"https://projet-eee.eu/coin-philo/projet-eee.levinasPhF.pdf"},{"title":"411 visage","url":"https://dev.prieenchemin.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/411-visage.pdf"}]},"I've performed the web search for your query about Levinas's concepts regarding the face of the other ("Le visage d'autrui"), denying the face ("nier son visage"), and treating the other as an object ("Traiter autrui comme un objet").

The search results provide relevant passages from Levinas's philosophy. Here are some key findings:

**On the relationship between the face and treating the other as an object:**

When you see and can describe a nose, eyes, forehead, and chin, you turn toward the other as toward an object. The best way to encounter the other is to not even notice the color of their eyes.

**On the ethical nature of the face:**

Levinas states: "The manner in which the Other presents itself, surpassing the idea of the Other in me, we call, indeed, the face" (Totalité et Infini).

**On the face's resistance to possession:**

The face refuses possession and my powers. In its epiphany, in expression, the sensible, though still grasping, transforms into total resistance to seizure.

**On the significance of the face:**

The face is significance without context. The other in the rectitude of their face is not a character in a context. The face is meaning by itself.

These passages illustrate Levinas's central argument that recognizing the other as a face (not as an object) is fundamentally an ethical act that precedes and transcends objectifying knowledge."],"durationSeconds":6.358535959001631,"searchCount":1}

input: {"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/popper/","prompt":"Popper falsifiability: is it a criterion for theories (demarcation) rather than tests? Does he say anything about the 'hazard of refutation' / 'game of science' quote? Disputes (Lakatos, Kuhn, Duhem-Quine)? Short paraphrase."}
result: {"bytes":118135,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Popper on Falsifiability: Criterion vs. Tests

## Falsifiability as Demarcation Criterion

Popper uses falsifiability primarily as a **demarcation criterion**—a tool to distinguish science from non-science. A theory is scientific if it's logically incompatible with possible observations; if compatible with all observations, it's unscientific. This addresses the core philosophical problem rather than individual experimental outcomes.

## Logic vs. Methodology

Popper explicitly distinguishes between the **logic** of falsifiability (theoretically simple: one counter-instance refutes universal laws) and its **applied methodology** (practically complex: scientists retain theories despite anomalies due to observational bias and measurement error).

## "Game of Science" / Hazard of Refutation

The document doesn't contain this specific quote. However, it describes Popper's emphasis on "critical thinking" as science's essence and his four-step deductive testing procedure where theories face potential falsification.

## Major Disputes

**Lakatos**: Denies critical tests exist. Argues high-level theories resist falsification through "protective belts" of auxiliary hypotheses; they're falsified through research programmes grinding to a halt, not isolated observations.

**Kuhn**: Challenges linear knowledge growth; proposes incommensurable paradigms instead of Popper's progressive accumulation model.

**Duhem-Quine problem**: Auxiliary hypotheses (not just universal laws) bridge theory-prediction gaps, making it unclear whether falsification targets the theory or auxiliaries.","durationMs":4904,"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/popper/"}

result: {"bytes":151693,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Kierkegaard's Indirect Communication Strategy

## Core Concept

Kierkegaard employed pseudonymous authorship and indirect communication as deliberate philosophical methods. He believed ethical and religious truths "cannot be directly or immediately communicated to others" and require what he termed "double reflection."

## The Socratic Connection

Drawing from his hero Socrates, Kierkegaard rejected didactic instruction. Rather than stating truths outright, he created pseudonymous characters embodying different existential perspectives—the aesthete, ethicist, and religious believer—allowing readers to encounter these viewpoints experientially rather than abstractly.

## Purpose and Method

The strategy aimed to discourage "purely verbal understanding" and encourage genuine appropriation. By presenting competing worldviews through distinct voices, Kierkegaard hoped readers would "come to understand their own lives better, in much the same way as encountering the characters in a great novel."

## The Point of View Explained

In *The Point of View for My Work as an Author* (written 1848, published posthumously), Kierkegaard claimed his entire authorship—pseudonymous works included—served religious ends. He sought to cultivate "inwardness" or "subjectivity" as prerequisites for authentic faith, positioning indirect communication as essential to this transformative project.

## Notable Disputes

Scholars debate whether *The Point of View* represents Kierkegaard's honest intentions or later revisionism, with critics arguing journals reveal a more complicated authorial evolution than his explicit claims suggest.","durationMs":5335,"url":"https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kierkegaard/"}

## Presentation of Self and Dramaturgical Theory

Goffman believed that we use impression management to present ourselves to others as we hope to be perceived. Goffman takes heavily from dramaturgical framework, analogizing social life to a theater, where individuals are "actors" who assume specific "roles" within "settings" (or "stages").

## Front Stage and Back Stage

The "front stage" represents the observable aspects of our performance, where we consciously manage our impressions, consisting of our appearance, demeanor, and surroundings. The "back stage," on the other hand, is where individuals can unwind their displays and be more genuinely, where we get ready for our front stage displays and contemplate on our interactions.

## Impression Management

Impression management refers to the conscious and unconscious processes through which individuals attempt to control the perceptions others form about them, and Goffman argues that this process is vital to social interaction. Goffman suggests that individuals often tailor their presentation of self depending on their audience, creating different versions of themselves for different social groups.
